evals.name: revise-cluttered-business-explainer
evals.prompt:
Can you tighten this for me? It's a draft of a blog post I'm putting on our company site.

---

In today's fast-paced business environment, it has become increasingly clear that the importance of effective communication cannot be overstated. Due to the fact that our customers are essentially inundated with a virtually endless stream of marketing materials on a daily basis, it is absolutely critical that we, as a company, make a concerted effort to ensure that our messaging is, in a very real sense, both clear and compelling.

With this in mind, we have made the decision to implement a number of new initiatives that are designed to facilitate improved communication outcomes across all of our various customer touchpoints. These initiatives include, but are not limited to, the development of a comprehensive new content strategy framework, the rollout of an enhanced customer feedback mechanism, and the implementation of a series of training modules for our customer-facing personnel.

It should be pointed out that these changes will be implemented in a phased manner over the course of the next several months. We are quite excited about the potential impact that these initiatives could potentially have on our overall customer experience metrics, and we look forward to sharing updates with all of our stakeholders as we progress through the various phases of implementation.

In conclusion, it can be noted that effective communication is, at the end of the day, one of the most important factors in determining the success of any business operation. We are committed to continuing to invest in this area as we move forward into the future.

---

This needs to go up next week. Make it actually good.
evals.expected_output: A revised draft that is dramatically shorter (likely 50%+ word cut), with active verbs, concrete nouns, killed throat-clearing phrases ('due to the fact that', 'it should be pointed out', 'in conclusion'), removed inflated Latinate words (implement, facilitate, virtually, essentially), a real lead replacing the 'In today's fast-paced...' opener, and an actual ending instead of 'In conclusion...'. Should include a short 'cuts made' notes section.

evals.name: draft-personal-essay-from-brief
evals.prompt: Help me write a short personal essay (about 600-800 words) about learning to bake sourdough during the pandemic. I want it to feel honest, not like one of those 'pandemic hobby' listicles. The angle: I was bad at it for a long time and what I learned wasn't really about bread. Audience is general readers — think a Sunday newspaper essay, not a food blog. First person, past tense.
evals.expected_output: A drafted essay that: (1) opens with a concrete specific image or moment, NOT 'In today's world' or 'Like many people during the pandemic'; (2) stays in first person and past tense consistently; (3) makes one clear point (not 'I learned X, Y, and Z'); (4) uses active verbs and concrete details over abstractions; (5) ends with finality — a callback, a vivid detail, or a quiet line — not a summary; (6) sounds like a person, not a content mill. Should be followed by a short notes section listing the pre-writing decisions (the one point, the attitude, etc.) so the user can redirect.

evals.name: fix-weak-lead-and-ending
evals.prompt:
I'm working on an op-ed for a local paper about why our city council should reject the proposed parking garage downtown. Here's what I have. I think it's roughly the right argument but it feels flat. Can you help?

---

Webster's dictionary defines 'infrastructure' as 'the basic physical and organizational structures and facilities needed for the operation of a society or enterprise.' When we think about infrastructure in our city, parking is often one of the first things that comes to mind.

The city council is currently considering a proposal to build a new $42 million parking garage on the corner of Main and 5th. Proponents argue it will solve downtown's parking shortage and boost businesses. I disagree.

First, downtown doesn't actually have a parking shortage. A 2024 study by the city's own transportation department found that on a typical weekday, our existing garages operate at only 61% capacity. The 'shortage' is really a problem of distribution — people want to park within 100 feet of their destination, which isn't realistic in any growing downtown.

Second, $42 million is a lot of money. That same amount could fund the long-promised expansion of the #14 bus route, build out the protected bike lane on Elm, or repave every residential street east of the river. Each of these would benefit far more residents than another parking garage.

Third, every successful downtown in the past twenty years has gotten that way by reducing car dependence, not by adding to it. Look at Burlington, look at Greenville. They tore garages down and built parks and apartments. Our council should learn from this.

In conclusion, the parking garage proposal is a bad idea. It solves a problem we don't have, costs money that could be better spent elsewhere, and runs counter to what works in other cities. I urge the council to vote no, and to instead invest in the kinds of infrastructure that will actually make our downtown thrive.

---
evals.expected_output: A revised op-ed with: (1) a new lead that is NOT the Webster's definition — should be a concrete fact, image, or paradox (e.g. the 61% capacity stat, the specific $42M cost juxtaposed with a concrete alternative, or a vivid image of the empty garage); (2) tighter sentence-level prose throughout (active verbs, cut hedges and qualifiers, cut 'in a typical weekday' style fillers); (3) a real ending that doesn't begin with 'In conclusion' — likely the kicker should land on a specific image or callback; (4) preserved structure of the three arguments but stronger transitions; (5) notes explaining the cuts.
